claims.text: Conventional cooling produces a broad distribution of nanoscale phase boundaries and a heterogeneous magnetic microstructure in the target rare-earth-free high-entropy alloy.
Rapid cooling followed by low-temperature annealing can increase the density of nanoscale phase boundaries while alloy composition remains constant.
The proposed processing can tune phase-boundary spacing to approximately the magnetic domain-wall width.
The relevant phase-boundary spacing is on the order of the magnetic exchange length and approximately equal to the magnetic domain-wall width.
Microstructural features smaller than or comparable to the exchange length reduce effective local magnetic anisotropy through exchange averaging or exchange softening.
Reduced local magnetic anisotropy facilitates coherent magnetic-domain switching.
An interconnected network of nanoscale phase boundaries enhances heat transfer.
Exchange-softened nanoscale phase boundaries sharpen the magnetic transition.
Engineering the nanoscale phase-boundary structure lowers magnetic hysteresis and associated energy loss.
Engineering the nanoscale phase-boundary structure maintains the alloy's mechanical robustness.
Relative to conventionally processed samples with coarser phase boundaries, the modified samples will have a stronger magnetocaloric response at low applied fields.
Relative to the baseline, the modified samples will exchange heat more rapidly.
Relative to the baseline, the modified samples will exhibit significantly reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the baseline, the modified samples will retain or improve mechanical integrity.
The hypothesis should apply to rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys dominated by ferromagnetic 3d elements.
The hypothesis is limited to near-room-temperature magnetic transitions and low applied fields typical of magnetic refrigeration.
Holding composition constant while changing thermal processing provides a controlled comparison of the proposed microstructural effect.
